title: Version 5 states one ACE service, one repository, one recovery module and one schema, which Architecture v5 replaces with 19 services
source: Recovery Workbench Engineering Practices v5; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1; Recovery Workbench Microservice Story Template and Rules v1
section: Section 2.1 One service, three modules; section 2.2 Boundary rules; section 1 Structure; section 7 Gate 6; section 6 Module boundary
description: Version 5 is written for one deployable: one service, one repository, one front end and one recovery module, with module boundaries checked in the build and with modules sharing one PostgreSQL database. Architecture v5 and the realignment cut Recovery into 19 services inside ACE, each with its own repository, schema and login. Architecture v5 wins on source precedence (R3, item 1 over item 9), so version 6 replaces the module boundary with the service and schema boundary and records the loser here.
evidence: Version 5 section 2.1: 'There is one service, one repository and one front end'; section 1 Structure: 'Modular monolith: common, collection and recovery modules by folder'; section 2.2: 'Each module owns its tables. Another module reads them only through the owning module's interface'; Architecture v5 slide 37 lists 'recovery-core: one deployable (ADR-001)' becoming '19 services, one per BA module' and 'One schema for everything (ADR-002)' becoming 'ACE database, one schema and login per service'; Template and Rules R4 gives 19 services and ADR-013 to ADR-014 record the decision.
proposed: Keep the conflict row closed by D-RCV-60 and retire the module wording at the next review, so that no later document repeats the one service position.

title: No source states how the built recovery schema, 92 tables and 14 data products, is cut across the 19 rwb_* schemas or how each V0001 baseline is produced
source: Recovery Workbench Engineering Practices v5; Recovery Workbench Microservice Story Template and Rules v1; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1
description: Version 5 assumes one recovery schema and one migration path. The realignment makes each service run its own Flyway sequence in its own schema, and R6 keeps the built Epic 1 migration while making the split into rwb_* schemas new work (RWB-PLT-NF06-DB and the per-service DB stories). No source read for this document states how the tables of the built schema are assigned to the 19 schemas, whether each service baseline is generated from the built schema or hand cut, or how the existing rows move, so the document states the practice and leaves the cut open.
evidence: Template and Rules R6: 'In build: the single recovery schema (92 tables, 14 data products, dictionary). The built migration is kept. The split into rwb_* schemas is new work (RWB-PLT-NF06-DB and the per-service DB stories)'; Architecture v5 slide 29: 'Each service runs its own Flyway migrations'; Architecture v5 gives no table of the built schema to schema cut; the Ownership Map v1 Tables sheet assigns 87 table rows to service owners but gives no migration order and no cut rule.
proposed: Add one cut table, built schema table to rwb_* schema with its baseline migration and its data move order, to the Physical Schema folder, and cite it from RWB-PLT-NF06-DB and from each per-service DB story.

title: No source names the 19 service repositories, their source-control group or the way an empty repository is provisioned
source: Recovery Workbench Engineering Practices v5; Recovery Workbench Microservice Story Template and Rules v1; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1
description: The realignment gives every service its own repository, created from the service template of RWB-PLT-TPL, with one code owners file in each. No source read for this document gives a repository name, a group or project in the bank source control, or the provisioning route, so version 6 states the rule and names each repository after its service until the convention is stated.
evidence: Template and Rules R5.1: 'RWB-PLT-TPL: service template and repositories'; Architecture v5 slide 38 note: 'one Helm chart, one golden pipeline'; the v5 document names 'one repository' only, with no name; Architecture v5 names no repository, group or project and no source-control product beyond the Helm chart and pipeline statements. The Ownership Map v1 Services sheet gives service, schema, REST base, topic and queue but no repository.
proposed: State the repository naming convention and the source-control group, provision the 19 empty repositories with branch protection and a code owners file from the service template, and add the repository name to the Services sheet of the Ownership Map.

title: The four DEV and two SIT deployment slots of version 5 are not stated per service now that there are 19 services with an api and a worker each
source: Recovery Workbench Engineering Practices v5; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1
section: Section 7 Pipeline gates, deployment slots paragraph
description: Version 5 counts four planned DEV slots and two SIT slots for one deployable. The realignment deploys about 38 small deployments, one api and one worker per service, so the slot count per service and the way a later wave gets a slot are not stated. Version 6 keeps the four and two figures of version 5, keeps DL35, and leaves the per-service slot model open rather than inventing one.
evidence: Version 5 section 7: 'ACE has four deployment slots planned in DEV and two in SIT, so squads can test in parallel. One slot in each is available today; the rest are being provisioned (DL35)'; Architecture v5 slide 49 note: 'about 38 small deployments at rest (most workers idle at minimum)'; no source read gives a slot per service or a wave-to-slot rule.
proposed: Publish the per-service deployment slot plan for DEV and SIT with the wave each service starts in, and replace the four and two figures with that plan when it exists.

title: No source states who approves a published contract version or where the contract artefact is held for its consumers
source: Recovery Workbench Engineering Practices v5; Recovery Workbench Microservice Story Template and Rules v1; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1
section: Section 2.4 Contract first; section 1 Contracts row
description: The realignment makes the contract the first thing a service publishes, and a change that is not backward compatible takes a new version and an ADR. No source read states who approves a contract version, how a consumer is told that a new version exists, or where the published OpenAPI, AsyncAPI and contract jar are held. Version 6 records the contract in the Service Contract Catalog v1 and in the service's API Specification file as the run material and leaves approval and publication open.
evidence: Architecture v5 slide 11: 'Every service publishes its contracts (OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, activity jar) before code; contract tests run in every build'; Template and Rules R8.4 lists 'Service Contract Catalog v1' and 'API Specification split into 19 files plus gateway-bff and an index' as run outputs; no source read names a contract approver, a review step or a published artefact store.
proposed: Name the contract approver role and the artefact store, add a contract review step to the CON story, and record the approved version in the Service Contract Catalog.

title: The Ownership Map v1 gives rwb-valuation no table, so its schema and its first migration have no listed content
source: Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5 Text Extract v1
description: Every service runs its own Flyway sequence in its own schema, so each service needs at least a baseline. The Tables sheet of the Ownership Map v1 has no row for S1 rwb-valuation, while it gives S1 three REST operations and a workflow; under the per-service Flyway rule the service would own no table. Version 6 states that its schema starts with its baseline only and leaves the ownership of a valuation table open.
evidence: Ownership Map v1 Tables sheet: 87 table rows, none with owner S1; sheet Endpoints: three rows with owner S1; sheet Workflows and activities: RouteDecisionWorkflow with owner S1; Architecture v5 slide 41 gives rwb-valuation the schema rwb_valuation and slide 19 gives it the valuation and route service, with no table list; Template and Rules R5.7 rule 7 requires every service to have a contract story, not a table.
proposed: Decide whether rwb-valuation keeps a table of its own, for example a route decision or valuation snapshot table, and add the row to the Tables sheet and to the rwb_valuation.sql file.

title: No approval of version 6 is recorded and the source carries no Status row
section: Metadata table; the document carries no approval or sign-off section
description: The source has no status row and no approval record, and the realignment run takes no approval stop. Version 6 therefore carries Status Draft and states that no approval is recorded, with the open approval carried here and in the assumption row.
evidence: The version 5 metadata table has five rows only: Document, Version, Date, Prepared by and Applies to. The document contains no approval, sign-off or status statement and ends at section 11.
proposed: Record the approval of version 6 by the solution architect, the ACE team and the programme, with a date, and keep a Status row with the approver role in every later version.

title: The source carries no change log and no tool line
section: Section 12 Change log; the source has no change-log section
description: Version 5 has a metadata table only and no change log, so there is no record of what changed between version 4 and version 5 and no tool line for the source. Version 6 adds the change-log table, records version 5 as the source row with the gap and the assumption, and gives its own row the D-RCV-60 change and the tool line.
evidence: The version 5 document ends at section 11 Assumptions and gaps and contains no change-log table, no revision history and no tool line; the converted text of the file has 11 numbered sections.
proposed: Add a change-log table to every later version and reconstruct the rows of versions 4 and 5 from the document properties and the release record.
